newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan campaign trail hits the Information Highway.
newsitem.headline: Japan campaign trail hits the Information Highway.

text.p: The scramble for votes in Japan's general election on Sunday has spilled over onto the information superhighway, with parties trying to attract support via the Internet.
Major parties began riding the Internet craze sweeping Japan by launching their own Web sites early this year.
Many redesigned their home pages on the Net after the election was announced last month. By some estimates, 30 million of the 98 million eligible voters are still undecided.

The home page of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) (http://www.sphere.ad.jp/ldp/) features its main campaign platform, promising stability and gradual reforms in the bureaucracy and tax overhauls.
A popular LDP section is the "Political Challenge" quiz, the party says. One question asks which politician is best at kendo, or Japanese swordfighting.
An LDP spokesman refused to give the answer but did reveal that it is not Hashimoto, who is shown in swordfighting garb in some of the party's campaign advertisements.
An LDP spokesman said users of its Internet page have doubled every month since it was introduced in January. In September there were some 180,000 retrievals.
A cartoon of a smiling Ichiro Ozawa, leader of the main opposition party Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), greets users of its home page (http://www1.meshnet.or.jp/NFP/).
The page features Ozawa's promises of huge income tax cuts, halving the bureaucracy and freezing a three percent sales tax.
A Shinshinto spokesman said it has retrievals of more than 100,000 a month.

Even the fledgling Democratic Party opened a Web site (http://dpj.smn.co.jp/) after leaders Yukio Hatoyama and popular Health Minister Naoto Kan launched the party last month. Their page is now one of the top choices among Japan's Internet users, registering as many as 10,000 viewers per day since the start of October.
It highlights the party's policy of slashing what it calls the bloated and overpowerful bureaucracy, but on a lighter note users can find out the favourite meal or even the blood type of its leaders.

A more serious Web site is provided by the Social Democratic Party (http://www.omnics.co.jp/politics/SDPJ/), where veteran Takako Doi resumed the helm after stepping down as speaker of the Lower House. The pros and cons of the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty are discussed in detail and the page also features a protest against nuclear testing.

"We have tried to make our home page interesting by providing more pictures and sound bites instead of putting in boring political debates all the time," said the party's Internet official Ryuji Yagi. He said several thousand viewers look at its page every month.
Sakigake (http://www.coara.or.jp/(tilde)sakigake/), a member of the ruling coalition, has a home page linking up with Web sites of other political parties and news media in Japan.

The Japan Communist Party boasts one of the most popular Web sites (http://www.infoweb.or.jp/jcp/index.html), seen by 300,000 people a month. Articles from party organ Akahata criticising the government are among its main features.
"We also get mail from overseas commenting on our home page," said Kenichi Ohtsuka, head of its Internet Desk. "The number of users has risen rapidly during the election campaign."
